newsitem.title: BURMA: Suharto ends Burma visit to strengthen ties.
newsitem.headline: Suharto ends Burma visit to strengthen ties.

text.p: Indonesian President Suharto ended a three-day visit to Burma on Sunday that focused on cementing stronger relations between the two nations without dwelling on political or human rights issues, officials said.
Hundreds of well-wishers wearing bright, colour-coordinated sarongs lined the road leading to the airport to wave Indonesian flags at Suharto as they bade him farewell on Sunday morning.
Suharto was accompanied at the airport by Burmese prime minister and head of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), Senior General Than Shwe.

Suharto's visit to Burma -- the last stop on a week-long, three-nation tour that included Cambodia and Laos -- comes amid questions over the acceptance of Burma as a full member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

The seven member nations of ASEAN have been pressured by several of their Western trading partners not to accept Burma as a full member until the SLORC improves its human rights record and agrees to talk with the democracy movement.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Burma, Cambodia and Laos are due to join the group soon although a date has not been set.
Burmese democracy leader, Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, has also urged ASEAN to rethink its plan to allow Burma to become a full member.

She says her National League for Democracy Party (NLD), which was never allowed to rule despite winning a landslide victory in a 1990 election, has been repeatedly harrassed by the SLORC and rights violations are continuing. She also urged all nations not to invest in Burma until the situation improves.
Although some analysts said there could have been an opportunity for Suharto to broach the subject with Burma's military leaders during his visit, few expected it.
Indonesia faced its own opposition in a recent meeting between Asian and European Union nations over its record in the former Portuguese colony of East Timor.

Indonesian officials said Suharto's visit to Burma -- his first in 23 years -- was mainly to improve economic ties between the nations, and Indonesia had no intention of interfering in Burma's internal affairs.

Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told reporters on Saturday that Suharto and top Burmese leaders had discussed Rangoon's entry into ASEAN and Indonesia had reaffirmed its desire to see that happen as soon as possible.
Alatas said Suharto and other top Indonesia officials discussed the issue of ASEAN during their visits to all three future ASEAN member nations over the past week.
He said all three appear to be well on the road to meeting requirements in order to become full members.
"I think the process is well underway. No date has been mentioned. As far as Indonesia is concerned...we see no difficulty in having the three as soon as possible."
He said the three nations would likely negotiate some extension regarding the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) by 2003. He said details regarding other deals were still to be worked out.
"I can't seen now whether there are any difficulties. Probably only some adjustments need to be made, with regard to AFTA entry and so on" he said.
